headline: High risk of data leakage and cascading errors: both agents handle secrets and shared MCP/browser workflows, while TREK’s collaborative defaults can amplify Nullclaw outputs into actions.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Nullclaw can ingest files, browser content, MCP, and shared workspace data; TREK also uses MCP and real-time collaboration. That creates a plausible instruction-injection bridge if TREK content is rendered or passed through shared channels. The pairwise pathway is inferred from documented surfaces, not directly observed, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF TREK content is forwarded into Nullclaw via MCP, files, or browser text without provenance checks, injection is possible.
IF either agent treats the other’s output as trusted instructions, prompt injection risk increases.
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of peer-generated text into tool prompts.
Add provenance tags to all MCP/file payloads.
Require a human review step before executing instructions extracted from shared content.
Restrict shared channels to read-only exports.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction-stripping at the orchestrator boundary.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Nullclaw explicitly handles API keys, private keys, bearer tokens, and workspace files, while TREK handles API keys, MFA secrets, reservations, and user accounts. Nullclaw has broad network egress and file access; TREK is collaborative and stores data in local files/logs. In default use, sensitive data can flow across the pair and out to external services, so high is warranted.
conditions: IF either agent shares workspace files or logs with the other, sensitive data can cross boundaries.
IF Nullclaw sends TREK-derived secrets to external APIs, leakage occurs.
IF TREK stores secrets in uploads or logs that Nullclaw reads, exposure occurs.
mitigations: Separate workspaces and credentials per agent.
Redact secrets before any cross-agent handoff.
Turn off broad egress for Nullclaw when handling TREK data.
Limit TREK uploads/logs to non-sensitive test data.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent secret-scoped storage and DLP controls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Nullclaw can write the filesystem, modify git state, and use MCP; TREK is collaborative and also uses MCP with shared mutable travel data. Their write surfaces overlap on files and possibly shared backend resources, but the profiles do not prove unrestricted writes to the same directory or git repo, so medium is the safest supported severity.
conditions: IF both agents target the same workspace or repository, write conflicts can occur.
IF both agents mutate shared MCP-backed state without locking, lost updates are possible.
mitigations: Assign separate directories and repos per agent.
Serialize writes through one coordinator.
Disable git mutation for one agent during joint runs.
Use file locks on shared mutable paths.
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency control to shared resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Nullclaw can generate browser, file, and MCP outputs; TREK is a real-time collaborative planner with AI built in, so it may treat upstream outputs as actionable travel facts. If TREK consumes Nullclaw output without verification, errors can cascade into reservations, budgets, or user-facing plans. The default collaborative workflow makes this dangerous enough for high.
conditions: IF TREK ingests Nullclaw-generated facts without validation, downstream plans can be wrong.
IF TREK uses those facts to update reservations or budgets, the blast radius expands.
mitigations: Require source citations on all transferred facts.
Add a verification step before TREK writes plans or bookings.
Mark Nullclaw outputs as untrusted by default.
Use a human approval gate for any action-taking step.
requires-engineering: implement schema validation and confidence thresholds on imported outputs.

E_compliance.rationale: Nullclaw touches audit logs, conversation history, and secrets; TREK touches reservations, country visit history, documents, and photos. The pair can therefore mix regulated personal data with different retention and residency expectations. No specific residency mismatch is proven, but the documented data classes and logging surfaces create a plausible compliance gap, so medium fits.
conditions: IF either agent retains logs containing personal data longer than the other’s policy allows, a retention mismatch exists.
IF travel documents or visit history are processed alongside CRM audit logs, subject-rights handling may diverge.
mitigations: Minimize logging of personal data in both agents.
Align retention windows before joint deployment.
Separate EU and non-EU datasets if applicable.
Review deletion/export workflows for both systems.
requires-engineering: add policy-aware data classification and retention enforcement.
